task.recognition: Recognition (a probe is shown; judge whether it is in memory)

task.reproduction: Reproduction / continuous report (reproduce a feature value such as a colour angle; also called delayed estimation or continuous recall)

metric.aggregate: Aggregate score (memorability score, hit / false-alarm rate)

notes: Each dataset is placed on three axes: how long the memory is held, what the task asks, and what kind of measurement is released.

Every metric table has the same four rows: people doing the task (Human), guessing (Random), the strongest released model, and the unified model (one model for every dataset, no dataset-specific parameters). A dash means the number was not measured or does not exist. For the datasets added in October 2026 the unified-model row so far shows trial-level AUC or NLL; the datasets' own metrics for the current model are being computed.
Published numbers were verified at source; figures are clipped from the original papers or author manuscripts for academic summary and carry their source and licence.

datasets.name: Wakeland-Hart scene memory
datasets.full: Wakeland-Hart, Cao, deBettencourt, Bainbridge & Rosenberg: scene memorability and attention
datasets.task_text: In Experiment 1, Amazon Mechanical Turk workers watched a stream of scene photographs (750 ms each, 800 ms apart) and pressed a key when an image repeated; target repeats came at least 30 s after the first showing. In Experiments 2 and 3, people in the lab sorted 500 scenes as indoor or outdoor (1 s each), then took an unannounced recognition test on studied and new scenes with a four-point confidence rating.
datasets.size: 706 web participants (Exp. 1) and 57 lab participants (Exps. 2-3), 1,100 scenes; about 149k responses (our build)
datasets.response: key press on repeats (Exp. 1); old / new with four-point confidence (Exps. 2-3)
datasets.paper: Wakeland-Hart, Cao, deBettencourt, Bainbridge & Rosenberg, Cognition 2022
datasets.metric_name: Per-image corrected recognition (Exp. 1) and within-person prediction of later memory (Exps. 2-3)
datasets.metric_intuition: First, whether the model ranks the scenes by memorability the way the web participants did. Second, for each lab participant, whether the scenes the model expects to be remembered with high confidence are the ones that person did remember.
datasets.metric_formula: CR = hit rate minus false-alarm rate per image over target images; rho = rank correlation between predicted and observed CR. Within-person r = point-biserial correlation, per participant, between the predicted probability of a 'sure old' answer and whether a studied scene got that answer; Fisher z averaged over participants and transformed back.

rows.method: Memorability and attention model (Wakeland-Hart et al. 2022)
rows.note: r: logistic regression on each scene's Exp. 1 memorability and the person's response time before the scene, trained on Exp. 2 and tested on Exp. 3, and the reverse; the paper does not predict memorability from the images

datasets.name: Recognition asymmetries
datasets.full: Utochkin, Chiang & Bainbridge: old / new and two-alternative recognition of the same 240 objects
datasets.task_text: Participants study 120 object photographs, each shown for 1 s with 0.5 s between them. One group then judges all 240 objects (the 120 studied and 120 new) as old or new; a second group sees 120 fixed pairs of one studied and one new object and picks the side of the studied one. Because each pair is tested with the roles swapped in the two study lists, the data show whether object A against object B is easier than B against A.
datasets.size: 397 participants (197 old / new, 200 forced choice), 240 objects; about 71k responses (our build)
datasets.stimuli: object photographs from the Massive Memory object set
datasets.response: old / new (per trial) or choice between two objects (per trial)
datasets.paper: Utochkin, Chiang & Bainbridge, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 2026
datasets.metric_name: Prediction of forced-choice d' and of its asymmetry across object pairs
datasets.metric_intuition: How well the predicted accuracy for each pair ranks the pairs the way people's accuracy does, and whether it also predicts which object of a pair is easier to pick as the studied one.
datasets.metric_formula: d' = sqrt(2) x z(proportion correct) for each pair and role assignment (240 values); asymmetry = d'(B studied, A new) minus d'(A studied, B new) for each of the 120 pairs; rho = rank correlation between predicted and observed values.

rows.note: split-half consistency, Spearman-Brown corrected: 0.68 for proportion correct, 0.72 for the asymmetry (the paper)
model that places every object, once as studied and once as new, on one familiarity scale using the hit and false-alarm rates of the separate old / new group

datasets.name: Symbol memorability
datasets.full: Roberts & Bainbridge: memorability of conventional symbols and of AI-designed novel symbols
datasets.task_text: In Experiment 1, web participants watched a stream of 80 everyday symbols such as $ or ? and pressed a key when one repeated; targets came back about 1.25 minutes later and attention checks a few symbols later. In Experiment 2, participants rated how well each of 40 new AI-generated symbols stood for a word, and after a 2-minute filler task judged 80 symbols as old or new; each new symbol had a 'memorable' and a 'forgettable' version designed from the features found in Experiment 1.
datasets.size: 577 participants (248 in Exp. 1, 329 in Exp. 2), 240 symbols; about 54k responses (our build)
datasets.stimuli: black-on-white symbols: 80 conventional, 160 generated with DALL-E 3
datasets.response: key press on repeats (Exp. 1); old / new (Exp. 2)
datasets.paper: Roberts & Bainbridge, PNAS 2026
datasets.metric_name: Variance in symbol memorability explained (Exp. 1) and the designed memorability effect (Exp. 2)
datasets.metric_intuition: First, how much of the spread in d' across the 80 conventional symbols a prediction accounts for. Second, whether symbols designed to be memorable are recognised better than their forgettable versions, as people did.
datasets.metric_formula: memorability of a symbol = recognition sensitivity d' = z(hit rate) minus z(false-alarm rate); R^2 = squared correlation between predicted and observed d' over the 80 symbols. Exp. 2: mean d' per participant for memorable and for forgettable symbols.

rows.note: Exp. 2 means over 329 participants (the paper); per-symbol d' in Exp. 1 has split-half consistency 0.69, Spearman-Brown corrected
in-sample regression on six components of participants' similarity sortings; image-only networks reach 0.18 (MemNet) and 0.07 (ResMem) in the same paper

datasets.task_text: Participants studied lists of 28 words shown one per second and then judged 50 test words: first old or new, then probably or definitely. Lists alternated between speed emphasis and accuracy emphasis, with feedback after each answer.

datasets.response: choice of one word among K, yes / no, or a set of words marked old (per trial)

datasets.name: Robison memory battery
datasets.full: Word recognition, cued recall and free recall from a two-session cognitive battery
datasets.task_text: Students did three verbal memory tasks as part of a 24-task battery, each task twice about two weeks apart: old / new recognition of 20-word lists (10 studied and 10 new words at test), cued recall of 10 word pairs (the first word is shown and the second must be typed), and immediate free recall of 10-word lists. The unified model is trained on the recognition and cued-recall answers; the typed free-recall outputs stay in each person's history as context only and carry no loss.
datasets.size: 272 participants tested, 255 in the paper's final sample; 251 participants, about 95k scored answers plus 39k free-recall outputs as context (our build)
datasets.stimuli: English words (six-letter words for recognition, unrelated four-letter word pairs for cued recall)
datasets.response: old / new key press; typed target word; typed free-recall words
datasets.paper: Robison, Campbell, Garner, Sibley & Coyne, Behavior Research Methods 2026
datasets.metric_name: Recognition accuracy and cued-recall accuracy
datasets.metric_intuition: How often a test word is correctly called old or new, and how often the paired word is recalled when its cue is shown.
datasets.metric_formula: recognition accuracy = correct old / new answers over answered test words, practice list excluded; cued recall = correctly typed targets over cued-recall tests, practice list excluded. Here an empty answer counts as not recalled, whereas the paper leaves unanswered tests out, so cued-recall values are lower than the paper's. Per participant and session, then averaged.

rows.note: computed on the held-out participants; the paper reports recognition 0.74 and 0.69 and cued recall 0.49 and 0.48 (first and second attempt; cued recall without unanswered tests)
no predictive model published; the paper is a study of reliability and factor structure

datasets.name: Judgments of learning
datasets.full: Judgments of learning with related and unrelated word pairs (17 experiments)
datasets.task_text: Participants study related and unrelated word pairs one at a time. In each experiment about half of them rate, right after each pair, how likely they are to recall it later (0 to 100), and the other half only study; a cued-recall test follows, in which the first word of each pair is the cue for the second. The unified model is trained on both the ratings and the recall answers.
datasets.size: 1,942 participants in 17 experiments; about 48k ratings and 106k recall tests (our build; the words of each pair are not in our build, only which pair it is)
datasets.stimuli: word pairs in German, Hebrew or English
datasets.response: rating from 0 to 100; recalled or not (per pair)
datasets.paper: Undorf, Ingendahl & Halamish, Collabra: Psychology 2024
datasets.metric_name: Reactivity of recall to making judgments, and resolution of the judgments
datasets.metric_intuition: Reactivity: how much making ratings changes later recall, comparing the group that rated with the group that only studied. Resolution: whether the pairs a person rates higher are the ones that person later recalls.
datasets.metric_formula: reactivity = proportion recalled in the rating group minus in the study-only group, within each experiment, then averaged over experiments (the authors report it separately for related and unrelated pairs, as Hedges' g). Resolution = Goodman-Kruskal gamma between a person's ratings and recall, per participant, then averaged.

rows.note: computed on the held-out pairs; the authors' meta-analysis of the 17 experiments finds g = +0.33 for related and -0.37 for unrelated pairs, a split our build does not record

figure.title: Factorial Comparison of Working Memory Models
figure.authors: Ronald van den Berg, Edward Awh, Wei Ji Ma
figure.caption_short: Example trial procedure in delayed estimation of color: subjects view a set of colored items, and after a brief delay report the color of one probed item by clicking on a color wheel.
figure.license: publisher copyright (© 2014 American Psychological Association) — author self-archived copy of the published version from the Ma lab website (cns.nyu.edu/malab); used under fair use for academic summary
figure.notes: Cropped from page 3 (journal page 126) of the published APA typeset PDF at 440 dpi; caption text excluded. Figure 2 is the paper's schematic of the delayed-estimation paradigm (memory array -> delay -> continuous report on a color wheel). The delayed-estimation benchmark analysed in this paper pools 10 previously published experiments (Table 1, same page): E1 Wilken & Ma 2004 (color wheel, Caltech); E2 Zhang & Luck 2008 (color wheel, UC Davis); E3 Bays et al. 2009 (color wheel, UCL); E4 Anderson et al. 2011 (orientation 360deg, U Oregon); E5 Anderson & Awh 2012 (orientation 180deg, U Oregon); E6 Anderson & Awh 2012 (orientation 360deg, U Oregon); E7-E9 Van den Berg et al. 2012 (color scrolling, color wheel, orientation 180deg; Baylor); E10 Rademaker et al. 2012 (orientation 180deg, Vanderbilt). Combined: 164 subjects, 131,452 trials. Figure 2 illustrates the color-wheel version; orientation experiments used an analogous continuous report. Data and code: https://github.com/WeiJiMaLab/delayed_estimation_benchmark. The PMC author-manuscript version is PMC4159389 (its PDF is behind a proof-of-work challenge; the Ma lab copy was used instead — note the task brief cited PMC3949221, but Unpaywall/PMC resolve DOI 10.1037/a0035234 to PMC4159389).

datasets.name: Change detection with change rates
datasets.full: Rouder, Morey, Cowan et al. single-probe colour change detection with three change rates
datasets.task_text: Two, five or eight coloured squares are shown for half a second, followed by a blank and a pattern mask; then a single square appears at one of the studied locations and the participant answers whether its colour is the same or different. Within each block of 60 trials the chance of a change is 30%, 50% or 70%, and this rate is shown to the participant before every trial.
datasets.size: 23 participants, 12,420 trials in the release; 12,385 responses with a valid key within 5 s (our build)
datasets.stimuli: coloured squares from a set of ten colours
datasets.paper: Rouder, Morey, Cowan, Zwilling, Morey & Pratte, PNAS 2008
datasets.metric_name: Accuracy and memory capacity K
datasets.metric_intuition: How often the same / different judgement is right, and how many squares that performance implies were held in memory once the tendency to answer 'different' is taken out.
datasets.metric_formula: K = N x (hit rate minus false-alarm rate) for a display of N squares tested with a single square (Cowan's formula, Eq. 3 of the paper); reported at N = 8, pooling the three change rates. Per participant, then averaged.

rows.note: held-out participants; the paper reports accuracy 0.945 with two squares and a capacity of 3.35 items from its fitted model

rows.method: Fixed-capacity model with attention (Rouder et al. 2008)
rows.note: fitted per participant and preferred by AIC, BIC and normalised maximum likelihood; per-trial numbers not published

datasets.name: Colour whole report
datasets.full: Ngiam, Loetscher & Awh whole report of six colours (colour-only condition)
datasets.task_text: Six coloured discs are shown for 500 ms (150 ms in Experiment 2). After a one-second blank, six empty placeholders appear and the participant reports the colour of every item, in an order of their own choosing, by clicking a placeholder and picking one of the eight colours from rings that appear around it; reported colours stay in view until all six are done.
datasets.size: 120 participants in four experiments in the release; the colour-only condition of Experiments 1, 2 and 4: 90 participants, 27,000 trials, 162,000 single-colour reports (our build)
datasets.response: one of eight colours for each of the six items, in the participant's own order
datasets.paper: Ngiam, Loetscher & Awh, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 2024
datasets.metric_name: Items correct per trial
datasets.metric_intuition: How many of the six colours a person reports correctly on a trial; in this study people averaged about three of the six.
datasets.metric_formula: items correct = number of the six reports that match the shown colour, averaged over trials (6 x the proportion of correct reports); per participant, then averaged. The model's value is the sum over the six reports of its predicted probability of the shown colour.

rows.note: held-out participants; the paper reports 3.21, 2.94 and 3.61 items in Experiments 1, 2 and 4
one of eight colours at random

rows.method: Partial-drop capacity model (fitted in the paper)

datasets.name: Colour localisation
datasets.full: Singh, Mihali, Chou & Ma search in visual working memory (two-location colour localisation)
datasets.task_text: Two, four, six or eight coloured discs appear for 100 ms at eight fixed places on a circle around fixation. After a one-second delay, two of the discs are replaced by empty grey circles and one of the two missing colours is shown at the centre; the participant clicks the circle where that colour had been.
datasets.size: 14 participants, 8,960 trials (640 each)
datasets.stimuli: coloured discs from a circle of 180 colours
datasets.response: choice of one of two locations (per trial)
datasets.paper: Singh, Mihali, Chou & Ma, PsyArXiv preprint 2023
datasets.metric_name: Proportion correct
datasets.metric_intuition: How often the participant picks the location that held the cued colour; it falls as more discs are shown and rises as the two candidate colours differ more.
datasets.metric_formula: proportion correct = correct choices / trials; per participant, then averaged. The model's value is its mean predicted probability of the correct location.

rows.note: all 14 participants, computed from the released data (0.93, 0.85, 0.76 and 0.69 with two, four, six and eight discs); no participant is held out in our split
